newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa announces landmark Telkom privatisation.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa announces landmark Telkom privatisation.

text.p: South Africa is set to clinch the largest privatisation deal in Sub-Saharan Africa with a landmark announcement on Monday that a stake in state-run telecommunications group Telkom will be sold to a U.S. and Malaysian consortium.

The Posts, Telecommunications and Broadcasting Ministry said it would now begin final negotiations for the sale of a 30 percent stake in Telkom with SBC Communications Inc and Telekom Malaysia Bhd following the closure of bidding last Friday.
"Negotiations will proceed solely with SBC Inc and Telekom Malaysia," the ministry said in a statement.
The final outcome is expected on schedule by early April.

The ministry said France Telecom had expressed a desire to continue to participate in the partial privatisation but Deutsche Telekom AG -- seen by many analysts as a leading contender for the stake -- failed to submit a bid.

Deutsche Telekom's spokesman, Hans Ehnert, told Reuters in a telephone interview the company had decided against the Telkom deal although it would continue to eye development opportunities in South Africa.

"The South African market is a very interesting market for Deutsche Telekom and therefore we studied the opportunities there but finally we didn't submit a bid to the South African government," he said.
Declining any details, Ehnert added: "Deutsche Telekom remains committed to the development of the telecommunications market in South Africa."
A full announcement on the financial details of the transaction would only be made once negotiations are concluded, the ministry said.

Analysts have estimated the value of the 30 percent stake at over six billion rand ($1.35 billion), valuing Telkom at more than $4 billion -- which they said made it the largest privatisation in Sub-Saharan Africa.

The sale of Telkom shares is the first major step in the South African government's privatisation drive. Economists said the bulk of the proceeds were likely to go to Telkom to fund delivery of lines to previously-deprived black areas.
BOE Natwest economist Nick Barnardt said the exchequer was expected to receive 25 percent of the money, which in turn might be split between debt reduction and other development projects.
"I would be quite comfortable with government using 50 percent of the cash (it receives) for projects and other 50 percent for debt reduction. The country needs growth," he said.
Life assurer Sanlam's Jac Laubscher said he expected the Telkom deal to be negotiated in rand which would flow in possibly as two or three payments spread out over a year.
"The government will get rand. The foreign party will of course have to buy rand," he said.

"It's positive for foreign reserves surely. But in terms of its immediate effect on money markets and the exchange rate, the government and Reserve Bank will try to neutralise that as far as possible," Laubscher said.
SBC already has a presence in South Africa through its 15 percent stake in the cellular phone operator MTN.
The bids for the Telkom stake were handled by SBC Warburg in London.
